text:
Here are the strongest open-ear options for running, based on recent reviews from Runner's World, WIRED, SoundGuys, and RTINGS. Prices change often, so check the retailer before you buy.

**Best overall: Bose Ultra Open Earbuds**
- Clip-on design that aims sound at the ear canal, so less sound leaks out than with most open designs. Physical buttons are easy to use mid-run.
- About $199 on sale (list $299), per [Runner's World](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/g63667125/best-open-ear-headphones-for-running/) and [WIRED](https://www.wired.com/story/best-open-earbuds/).
- Tradeoffs: about 7 hours of battery per charge, IPX4 water resistance, and a higher price. Runner's World reports that Bose is releasing a successor within about a month, so you may want to wait.

**Best bone conduction: Shokz OpenRun Pro 2**
- Sends sound through your cheekbones and adds air-conduction bass, so it sounds fuller than older bone-conduction models. WIRED rates it 8/10 and calls it the best running option for bass and power ([WIRED review](https://www.wired.com/review/review-shokz-openrun-pro-2/)).
- About $180 list, with some retailers listing it around $125 ([Runner's World](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/g63667125/best-open-ear-headphones-for-running/)).
- Tradeoffs: about 12 hours of battery and IP55 water resistance. The neckband can interfere with long hair or hats, and it may not suit hooded or high-collared tops.
- RTINGS finds the Bose slightly better for most people, since it's more portable and doesn't press on the cheekbones and temples. The Shokz has a tougher rating and multi-device pairing ([RTINGS comparison](https://www.rtings.com/headphones/tools/compare/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-shokz-openrun-pro-2-bone-conduction/50264/72946)).

**Best for long runs: Shokz OpenDots 2**
- About $200. 10 hours per charge and 40 hours with the case, plus IP57 dust and water resistance ([WIRED](https://www.wired.com/story/best-open-earbuds/)).
- Runner's World calls it the best for long runs ([source](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/g63667125/best-open-ear-headphones-for-running/)).
- Tradeoff: no noise cancellation, and volume could be higher.

**Best for running (SoundGuys): Nothing Ear (Open)**
- SoundGuys names it its top running pick, citing strong bass for an open design, an IP54 rating, and a customizable EQ. It's about $99 on Amazon, down from $149 ([SoundGuys](https://www.soundguys.com/best-workout-earbuds-2719/)).

**Runner-up: Soundcore AeroClip**
- WIRED's runner-up: light, stable, and long-lasting, with about 8 hours of battery and IP55 resistance. It's about $130 on sale, and Soundcore has announced the AeroClip 2 ([WIRED](https://www.wired.com/story/best-open-earbuds/)).

**Budget picks**
- JLab Flex Open, about $40. A low-risk way to see whether clip-on open earbuds suit you ([Runner's World](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/g63667125/best-open-ear-headphones-for-running/)).
- Soundpeats PearlClip Pro, about $50. WIRED's best cheap option ([WIRED](https://www.wired.com/story/best-open-earbuds/)).
- Soundcore AeroFit 2, about $80 on Amazon. SoundGuys' best budget pick ([SoundGuys](https://www.soundguys.com/best-open-ear-headphones-and-earbuds-115102/)).

I also found a deal page for the AeroFit 2 at dealectric.com that cites a discount code. I couldn't verify the code, and that page is an affiliate listing, so check the price directly at Soundcore's checkout before relying on it.

**Choosing:** If you run on busy roads, go with bone conduction (OpenRun Pro 2) or a clip-on with good sound (Bose). If you want the best sound and don't mind the price, pick the Bose. For long runs and rain, pick the OpenDots 2. Whichever you choose, keep the volume low enough to hear traffic. Open designs don't block outside noise, so they don't guarantee safety.
